paper_title: Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires $32\times$ fewer retrieval queries and $2048\times$ fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.

Introduction Large language models (LLMs) (Yang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2026) have advanced rapidly in language understanding, generation, and reasoning. Their growing capabilities support knowledge-intensive applications, but reliable answers require facts that can be missing, poorly retained, or outdated in pretrained parameters (Lewis et al., 2020). Knowledge injection addresses this gap by incorporating information from an external corpus. central challenge is to incorporate this knowledge effectively while preserving existing capabilities and keeping knowledge acquisition and inference costs manageable. Existing approaches face different trade-offs in addressing this challenge. Continued pretraining (CPT) (Gururangan et al., 2020) learns from an additional corpus through language modeling, while LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) offers parameter-efficient way to adapt the model. These approaches keep inference self-contained, but adaptation can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired capabilities (Biderman et al., 2024). Non-parametric retrieval instead provides external evidence during generation. RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) conditions on retrieved passages, and RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022) incorporates retrieved chunks within the decoder. These methods provide access to corpus knowledge without first learning it in model parameters, but datastore search and evidence processing can add substantial inference latency (Cao et al., 2026).

sections.title: Deep Fusion Memory
sections.content: Parametric memory learns from retrieved knowledge offline, enabling inference without explicit retrieval. MLP Memory (Wei et al., 2026a) and Memory Decoder (Cao et al., 2026) learn to predict retrieval-derived next-token distributions. However, this inference advantage comes with substantial offline costs. Constructing token-level training targets requires retrieval at individual token positions across the corpus, resulting in substantial data construction costs (Wei et al., 2026b). Training memory modules on these targets further incurs significant computational cost. Moreover, these methods rely on shallow fusion through output-probability interpolation, without incorporating memory into the decoders hidden states. Intuitively, integrating memory into intermediate hidden states allows subsequent layers to further process and combine it with the evolving context. The broader challenge is to enable language models to acquire external knowledge efficiently and use it effectively. In this work, we introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), parametric memory architecture that combines efficient knowledge acquisition with deep fusion within the decoder (Figure 1). At high level, DFM shares memory supervision across multiple token predictions while allowing each token to use the learned memory according to its context. We jointly train memory predictor and memory fusion module, using retrieved target memory to supervise the predictor and the standard language modeling objective to train both modules. In this way, external knowledge is not only stored in the predictors parameters, but also injected into intermediate hidden states through the fusion module, allowing subsequent decoder layers to utilize the memory during generation. The LLM backbone remains frozen throughout, and memory prediction is performed at the chunk level. Our experiments demonstrate improvements in both efficiency and downstream performance. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches that construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires 32 fewer retrieval queries and 2048 fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. DFM achieves the highest average score across six QA tasks on both backbones, outperforming the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, adaptation across code, mathematics, and law yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively. Ablations further highlight the importance of fusion placement and gate initialization, while showing comparatively small changes in average QA performance across the tested chunk sizes and numbers of memory slots. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce DFM, parametric memory architecture with deep fusion, which integrates learned corpus knowledge into intermediate hidden states so that subsequent decoder layers can process memory together with the evolving context. Inference requires no explicit retrieval. We reduce the overhead of supervision construction and memory training through chunk-level supervision and end-to-end training with frozen backbone. For training data construction, DFM requires 32 fewer retrieval queries and 2048 fewer retrieved items than existing parametric memory approaches based on token-level targets. We demonstrate improved QA performance and domain adaptation. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8BBase. Across code, mathematics, and law, average gains over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base reach 6.51 and 4.38 points, respectively. 2. Related Work Model Adaptation. Continued pretraining adapts language models to additional corpora through further language modeling (Gururangan et al., 2020), while LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) offers parameterefficient way to adapt the model. Such adaptation can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired capabilities (Biderman et al., 2024). Deep Fusion Memory keeps the backbone frozen and

sections.content: learns an added memory module from retrieval-derived targets, jointly training memory prediction and fusion. Retrieval-Augmented Language Models. Non-parametric memory exposes corpus information through several interfaces. 𝑘NN-LM retrieves contexttoken pairs and interpolates neighbor-derived next-token distribution with the language model output (Khandelwal et al., 2019), whereas RAG conditions generation on retrieved passages (Lewis et al., 2020). RETRO combines chunk retrieval with cross-attention inside the Transformer (Borgeaud et al., 2022). xRAG projects retrieved document embedding into single token representation prepended to the query, reducing the context passed to the generator (Cheng et al., 2024). These methods retain an external retrieval dependency at inference. Deep Fusion Memory predicts continuous memory parametrically and uses it inside the decoder without online search. Parametric Memory. MLP Memory trains an MLP to predict 𝑘NN token distributions from language model representations (Wei et al., 2026a). Memory Decoder learns similar distributional target with standalone decoder (Cao et al., 2026). Memory Decoder at Scale extends this approach to large-scale general and domain memory pretraining (Wei et al., 2026b). MemSFT specializes frozen backbones through domain memory and learned token-wise router over the backbone and memory output distributions (Wang et al., 2026). These approaches avoid explicit retrieval at inference, but token-level retrieval incurs substantial data construction costs, and output-probability interpolation provides only shallow fusion. Deep Fusion Memory reduces the cost of supervision construction by sharing target memory across tokens within each chunk and fuses predicted memory into hidden states through gated cross-attention. 3. Deep Fusion Memory Deep Fusion Memory consists of causal chunk-level memory predictor and memory cross-attention modules inserted into selected decoder layers (Figure 1). We construct target memory offline, then jointly train the added modules with language-modeling and memory-prediction objectives while keeping the backbone frozen. At inference, the predictor supplies memory directly from the input sequence. 3.1. Training data construction We partition each training sequence into non-overlapping chunks 𝑋0, . . . , 𝑋𝐽1 of 𝐶 tokens. For each chunk 𝑋 𝑗 with 𝑗 1, an offline retriever encodes the preceding chunk 𝑋 𝑗1 and retrieves its top-𝐾 neighbors from corpus datastore. Each retrieved chunk is represented by fixed dense embedding produced by frozen text encoder. Stacking these embeddings in retrieval-rank order gives the target memory 𝑉𝑗 ℝ𝐾𝑑𝑚, where 𝑑𝑚 is the embedding dimension. This ordering aligns the target memory with the predictors output slots. Each training example pairs the original token sequence with its chunk-level target memory. Each target memory supervises the predictor output shared across token predictions in 𝑋 𝑗. Predictions for the first chunk use no memory, and this chunk is excluded from memory supervision because it has no preceding-chunk query. Target memory is prepared offline and remains fixed during model training. 3.2. Training Memory Predictor. The predictor generates 𝐾 continuous memory vectors for each chunk from the preceding context (Figure 1(a)). Let 𝑒𝑖 = 𝐸𝜃(𝑥𝑖) denote the embedding of token 𝑥𝑖 in the frozen

sections.content: The sigmoid gate 𝑔𝑡 (0, 1) 𝐻 assigns one scalar to each token and head, shared across all channels in the head. It scales the head output before concatenation and output projection. Attention selects information from the shared memory for each token, while the gate controls how much each head contributes. For token predictions in the first chunk, the memory update is zero. The memory branch runs in parallel with causal self-attention. Both outputs enter the same residual update: (cid:101)ℎ𝑡 = ℎ𝑡 + SelfAttn(𝑧𝑡) + 𝑢𝑡. The updated state (cid:101)ℎ𝑡 then passes through the original decoder feed-forward sublayer, including the associated normalization and residual connection. The memory predictor and memory projector are shared across fusion layers. Each fusion layer uses layer-specific memory-attention and gate projections, separate from the self-attention parameters. Other decoder layers retain their original computation. (3) Memory alignment follows next-token prediction. With zero-based token positions, the state at 𝑡 predicts 𝑥𝑡+1 and uses chunk index 𝑗 = (𝑡 + 1)/𝐶. At chunk boundary, the preceding chunk is complete before the pooled query is used. Together with the memory predictor, this ensures that memory generation uses only the input available for the next-token prediction. Joint Training Objective. (4) The MSE excludes 𝑋0, which has no preceding chunk. We set 𝛽 = 1. The MSE is computed directly against the L2-normalized target embeddings, without renormalizing the predictions. The language model consumes predicted memory throughout training. Target memory is used only for supervision. Gradients from LLM pass through memory fusion into the predictor, while LMSE directly supervises the predicted memory slots. The predictor, query projection, memory projector, cross-attention, and gate parameters are optimized jointly. The backbone, retrieval encoder, and target memory remain fixed. 3.3. Inference At inference, the language model uses the same predictor and fusion modules without constructing target memory. Chunk queries are formed from backbone input embeddings, and the memory predictor supplies predicted memory to the selected decoder layers. No datastore search, retrieved text, or external embedding encoder is required. For QA evaluation, predicted memory is computed from the visible prompt and remains fixed during answer generation. Selected decoder layers attend to the predicted memory only at positions associated with the prompt chunks. As defined in Eq. 2, sigmoid gate conditioned on the current token state scales each head before output projection. With layer-specific gate parameters, the contribution of the fixed memory can vary across tokens, heads, and layers. 4. Experiments We evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of DFM across knowledge-intensive question answering and domain adaptation. We first describe the datasets, training configurations, and baselines (4.1).

sections.title: Deep Fusion Memory
sections.content: We then evaluate DFM on six knowledge-intensive question-answering tasks (4.2) and examine its effectiveness beyond QA through domain adaptation in Code, Math, and Law (4.3). Finally, we compare parameter overhead, training time, and target-construction workload with token-level memory (4.4). 4.1. Experimental Setup Datasets. For question answering, we train on English Wikipedia from December 2018, comprising approximately 4B tokens. We evaluate single-hop QA on NQ (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) and WebQA (Berant et al., 2013), and multi-hop QA on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020), MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022), and Bamboogle (Press et al., 2023). For domain adaptation, we sample subsets from Swallow-Code (Fujii et al., 2026) and Swallow-Math (Fujii et al., 2026), and use legal text from DISC-Law-SFT (Yue et al., 2023). We evaluate Code on HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and HumanEval+ (Liu et al., 2023), Math on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and Law on LawBench (Fei et al., 2024). Appendices A.1 and A.2 give data-construction and evaluation details for QA and domain adaptation. Training Details. We use Mistral-7B-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023) and Qwen3-8B-Base (Yang et al., 2025) for question answering, and Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base (Yang et al., 2025) for domain adaptation. DFM uses 32-token chunks and target memory formed from the top-16 chunk embeddings retrieved using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025), with gated memory fusion at layers [9, 16, 24, 31]. The added modules contain 0.75B parameters on both QA backbones and 0.6B on Qwen3-4B-Base. We freeze the backbone and train the added modules for one epoch with next-token cross-entropy and memory-prediction MSE, using AdamW with learning rate 1 105. Wikipedia training uses 2,048-token sequences and global batch size of 128 on 16 A800 80GB GPUs. For domain adaptation, we train separate model for each domain with 262,144 tokens per optimizer update. Further architectural details and training configurations are given in Appendix A. Baselines. We compare against three non-parametric and three parametric baselines. Among nonparametric methods, RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) augments the input with the top-1 passage retrieved using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. xRAG (Cheng et al., 2024) projects retrieved documents dense embedding into single token prepended to the question. RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022) incorporates retrieved chunks through cross-attention. Among parametric methods, CPT updates all backbone parameters through continued pretraining for one epoch. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) trains low-rank adapters for one epoch, with its added parameter budget matched to DFM. MLP Memory (Wei et al., 2026a) learns to predict token-level kNN distributions from Wikipedia 2018 and interpolates its predictions with the backbones output probabilities. 4.2. Question Answering Performance Overall Performance. Table 1 compares DFM with non-parametric and parametric methods across six QA benchmarks. DFM achieves the highest average on both backbones without online retrieval. On Mistral, it raises the six-task mean from xRAGs 24.14 to 27.21, 12.71% relative improvement over the strongest baseline. On Qwen3-8B-Base, it improves from MLP Memorys 23.80 to 26.46, 11.19% relative improvement. These correspond to absolute gains of 3.07 and 2.66 points, showing comparable relative benefits across the two backbone families. Relative to Base, DFM gains 13.59 and 3.75 points, improving all six tasks on Mistral and five on Qwen3. It also outperforms CPT and LoRA on every Mistral task and five Qwen3 tasks. Single-Hop Question Answering. On Mistral, DFM reaches 33.57 on NQ and 42.47 on WebQA, improving over Base by 13.27 and 13.19 points. These scores exceed the strongest baseline on each

On Qwen3, NQ improves from 17.60 to 27.46, exceeding RAG by 3.04 points. WebQA instead decreases from 41.78 to 39.47, while MLP Memory achieves 43.26. The contrasting WebQA outcomes show that memory adaptation is not uniformly beneficial across backbones, even when the original weights remain frozen. Multi-Hop Question Answering. DFM improves over Base on all four multi-hop benchmarks for both backbones. On Mistral, it leads on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle, with Bamboogle increasing from 3.91 to 22.65. Its 2Wiki score rises from 5.87 to 25.00, although RAG remains stronger at 31.02. On Qwen3, DFM achieves the best results on 2Wiki, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle, including 7.55-point gain over Base on 2Wiki. It also improves HotpotQA to 26.46, below xRAGs 27.74. These results indicate that predicted memory can support tasks requiring multiple pieces of evidence, while explicit retrieval retains an advantage on some benchmarks.

Figure 2(b) compares these measured training costs. Appendix provides the timing details. Target Construction. Figure 2(c) shows that, for 4B-token corpus, token-level construction requires 4B retrieval queries, whereas 32-token chunks require 125M, 96.88% reduction. Each query produces one target entry. With Top-1024 for MLP Memory and Top-16 for DFM, the total number of retrieved items falls from 4B 1024 = 4.096T to 125M 16 = 2B, 99.95% reduction. By reducing both the number of retrieval queries and the neighbors returned per query, chunk-level supervision substantially lowers the retrieval overhead of target construction. 5. Ablations and Analysis We study chunk size, fusion-layer configurations, memory slots, and memory gating on Mistral-7Bv0.3 with predicted memory, varying one factor from the main configuration in Table 1. Figure 3 reports six-task QA averages. DFM is robust to the tested chunk sizes and slot counts, and to fusion configurations spanning intermediate and late layers. Appendix gives exact settings, task-level results, and additional ablations on learning rate, projector sharing, predictor depth, and prediction loss. Appendix presents QA and offline-retrieval case studies. 5.1. Ablation Studies Chunk Size. Figure 3(a) reports averages of 26.51, 27.21, and 27.07 for chunk sizes 16, 32, and 64, respectively. The 32-token setting performs best. Doubling the chunk size to 64 halves targetconstruction queries with only 0.14-point drop. The 16-token setting doubles retrieval queries without improving the mean, so finer-grained supervision is not necessarily more effective. This supports 32-token chunks as practical balance between QA performance and construction workload. Fusion Depth and Placement. In Figure 3(b), two to eight fusion layers starting at layer 9 achieve 27.0927.54, versus 21.11 with final-layer-only fusion and 22.07 with the final four layers. With four fusion modules, distributing memory access across intermediate and late layers is more effective than concentrating it near the output. Four, six, and eight fusion layers remain within 0.13 points of one another, supporting the four-layer default without consistent gain from greater fusion depth. The

These results favor intermediate-to-late fusion, as also used in RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022). possible explanation is that more developed semantic representations aid memory integration, with later layers processing the fused information. Number of Memory Slots. In Figure 3(c), 𝐾 values of 2, 4, 8, and 16 yield averages of 26.88, 27.04, 27.09, and 27.21. Top-16 exceeds Top-8 by only 0.12 points: Top-8 scores higher on five tasks, while Top-16 improves Bamboogle. Even Top-2 remains within 0.33 points of Top-16, indicating that DFM maintains similar average QA performance with substantially fewer memory slots. This makes smaller 𝐾 practical option for using fewer target vectors and reducing memory-attention computation while retaining similar average performance. 5.2. Memory Gating Table 3 examines the effect of token-wise, per-head gating on memory fusion and its sensitivity to initialization. Removing the gate reduces the six-task mean from 27.21 to 26.83, with the decrease driven mainly by Bamboogle and smaller, mixed changes on the other tasks. Initializing the gate bias at 0 yields the highest mean, 27.90, and improves five of six tasks over the no-gate variant, providing further support for gated fusion. More negative initial biases yield lower means in this sweep. We retain 𝑏𝑔 = 2 as conservative default: with zero-initialized gate weights, 𝜎(2) 0.119 initially scales down the memory branch to limit its perturbation to the pretrained backbone, while allowing the gate to adapt during training.

Conclusion We presented Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), parametric memory architecture that combines efficient supervision construction with deep fusion within the decoder. Sharing target memory across tokens in each chunk reduces retrieval work, while gated cross-attention allows subsequent decoder layers to process predicted memory together with the evolving context. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. DFM improves the six-task QA average over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, DFM improves performance over the base models across code, mathematics, and law. These results demonstrate that shared supervision and learned internal fusion can support efficient knowledge acquisition and effective memory use.

sections.title: Deep Fusion Memory
sections.content: A. Experimental Details A.1. Question Answering Data construction. We use section and infobox text from Wikipedia December 2018. Records are grouped by normalized article titles and assigned to training, validation, and test splits in proportions of 99.8/0.1/0.1% using seed 42. We remove exact text duplicates across splits, append EOS to each record, and pack records within each split into 2,048-token sequences. Incomplete final sequences are discarded. Tokenization yields 4.70B, 4.29B, and 4.08B training tokens for Mistral, Qwen3, and OLMo3, respectively. Each sequence is divided into non-overlapping 32-token chunks. We encode training chunks with the frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B encoder, using last-token pooling and L2 normalization to obtain 1,024-dimensional representations. FAISS IVF-PQ index supports offline neighbor retrieval. Following Section 3.1, each preceding chunk retrieves target memory for the next chunk. We retain the top-16 full chunk embeddings in retrieval-rank order, including the nearest neighbor, and mask the first chunk from memory supervision. The datastore contains training chunks only. Training. DFM freezes the backbone and jointly trains its chunk-level memory predictor, shared projector, and gated fusion modules. The predictor has 28 layers, hidden width 1,024, FFN width 3,072, 16 query heads, and eight KV heads. Its 16 output heads predict the continuous memory slots. The L2normalized targets have coordinates in [1, 1], and the predictor clips output coordinates to this range. Memory cross-attention is inserted at zero-based layers [9, 16, 24, 31], with gate weights initialized to zero and gate biases to 2. OLMo3 retains its original attention-output normalization. The objective combines next-token cross-entropy and raw memory-prediction MSE with equal weights. We train for one epoch on 16 A800 80GB GPUs, with one sequence per GPU and eight gradient-accumulation steps, giving global batch size of 128. AdamW uses learning rate 1 105, ( 𝛽1, 𝛽2) = (0.9, 0.999), 𝜖 = 108, zero weight decay, and gradient clipping at 1. We use 500 warmup steps followed by cosine decay, BF16 precision, seed 42, and the final checkpoint for evaluation. Baselines. RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) retrieves the top-1 document from Wikipedia training-corpus index using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and adds it to the question context. xRAG (Cheng et al., 2024) projects retrieved documents dense embedding into single token prepended to the question. RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022) uses chunk-level retrieval and cross-attention to incorporate retrieved text into hidden states. CPT updates all backbone parameters for one epoch on Wikipedia at learning rate 2 105. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) trains low-rank adapters for one epoch at the same learning rate of 2 105, with the added parameter budget matched to DFM. MLP Memory (Wei et al., 2026a) learns to predict token-level kNN distributions from Wikipedia 2018 and interpolates its predictions with the backbone probabilities. As in MLP Memory, interpolation weights are task-specific; we select the best 𝜆 {0, 0.05, . . . , 1} on each reported evaluation split. In the task order of Table 4, we use 𝜆 = (0.55, 0.55, 0.55, 1.00, 0.90, 1.00) for Mistral and (0.35, 0.45, 0.25, 0.80, 0.55, 0.00) for Qwen3. Evaluation. Table 4 summarizes the six QA benchmarks. DFM uses zero-shot greedy decoding without online retrieval, gold documents, or chain-of-thought demonstrations. Questions are formatted with task-specific questionanswer templates. Generation stops at newline or the token limit, with period and comma as additional stop strings for WebQA. Evaluation batches contain one example per GPU, except WebQA, which uses four. For QA, each memory query is formed from the current visible prompt chunk rather than the preceding chunk used during training. The queries and predicted memory remain fixed during generation. For newly added chunk positions, the adapter pads queries and query-validity masks with zeros, so these positions receive no direct memory update. Generated answer chunks do not refresh the queries, and incremental predictor caching is not used in the reported implementation. F1 measures normalized token overlap and takes the maximum over

Domain Adaptation Data. Code and Math each use 100M training tokens sampled from Swallow-Code and SwallowMath (Fujii et al., 2026), with document-level train/validation/test splits of 98/1/1%. Law uses 123.5M training tokens from DISC-Law-SFT (Yue et al., 2023), holding out 1% of source-train for validation. We preserve its Reference: field when present, together with Input: and Output:. We deduplicate documents, screen benchmark overlap through normalized exact matching, append EOS, and pack sequences within each split. Target memory is constructed as in Appendix A.1, using training-only datastores, 32-token chunks, and Top-16 retrieval. Training. We use the default DFM configuration for Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, with the backbone frozen and the same memory predictor, shared projector, fusion layers, and gate initialization as in the QA experiments. DFM uses learning rate 1 105, cosine decay, zero weight decay, and 11 warmup steps for Code/Math or 14 for Law. All adapted models train for one epoch in BF16 with 262,144 tokens per update. Sequence length is 8K for Code training on Qwen3-4B-Base and 2K for all other backbonedomain pairs. CPT and LoRA use the same data and sequence length as DFM. Both use learning rate 2 105, with 3% warmup and weight decay 0.1. LoRA uses rank 256, alpha 512, and zero dropout. We train separate checkpoint for each domain. RAG. RAG uses the frozen Base backbone without additional training. It retrieves the top-1 document from the corresponding domains training corpus using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. Retrieved Code is prefixed as comments, while Math and Law use background prefix. The original task prompt is preserved in full; only retrieved background is truncated when the input budget is exceeded. Few-shot examples, sample counts, generation settings, and scorers are identical to Base. Evaluation. HumanEval uses three demonstrations and four samples per problem, while HumanEval+ uses zero demonstrations and one sample. Code reports sample-average execution correctness, estimating pass@1. GSM8K uses eight demonstrations and one sample. LawBench evaluates 500 examples for each of its 20 tasks in the zero-shot setting. All methods use common Input:/Output: template without chat template, greedy decoding, and the official task scorers. The LawBench score is the equal-weight macro average of the 20 task metrics. Main-table Avg. equally weights HumanEval, HumanEval+, GSM8K, and LawBench. Appendix B.2 provides the per-task LawBench results for the same models.

They use predicted memory, frozen backbone, one training epoch, and the same six-task QA protocol. All results are single runs. C.1. Chunk Size, Fusion Placement, and Memory Slots Reference configuration. The reference for Figure 3 uses continuous predicted memory, 32-token chunks, target memory from Top-16 retrieval, shared projector, gate bias 2, and learning rate 1 105. Its fusion layers are [9, 16, 24, 31] (zero-based), and its six task scores match Table 1 exactly. These structural sweeps retain the other named architectural settings. Appendix A.1 gives the reference training recipe. Figure 4 Task-level score changes relative to the main DFM configuration on Mistral-7B-v0.3. Blue and brown indicate increases and decreases, respectively. Avg. gives the change in the unweighted six-task mean. Fusion labels denote the number of fusion layers, while Last four and Start layer 2 use [28, 29, 30, 31] and [2, 10, 21, 31], respectively. All differences are computed before rounding. Chunk size. Relative to 32 tokens, the 16-token setting improves 2Wiki and MuSiQue but decreases the other four scores. The 64-token setting improves 2Wiki by 1.03 points, with decreases of 0.031.08 on the other tasks. For fixed token budget, target-construction query counts scale inversely with chunk size. This establishes workload trade-off but does not measure elapsed construction time. Fusion depth and placement. Training costs compare measured training times on 16 A800 GPUs for both methods; retrieval counts use common 4B-token corpus. Table 13 Numerical accounting for the comparison in Figure 2. Construction counts assume common 4B-token corpus. Training hours are rounded measurements on 16 A800 GPUs for both methods. Quantity Added parameters (B) A800 GPUs Measured training hours Training GPU-hours Target queries Neighbors per query Returned neighbor slots MLP Memory DFM Basis 1.50 16 64 1,024 0.75 Configuration 16 Configuration 24 Timing 384 GPUs hours 4B 125M Workload count 1,024 4.096T 16 Configuration 2B Workload count Reference configurations. We use the 1.5B MLP Memory configuration (Wei et al., 2026a) throughout the experiments, including the parameter and training-time comparisons. DFM adds approximately 0.75B parameters, reduction of approximately 50%. Measured training time. Both methods are trained on 16 A800 GPUs using the same training corpus and number of epochs. Timings cover training only, excluding target construction and evaluation. MLP Memory takes approximately 64 hours, while DFM takes approximately 24 hours, corresponding to 1,024 and 384 GPU-hours. DFM therefore uses 24/64 = 37.5% of the training time, reduction of approximately 62.5%. All reported costs use these rounded training times. Construction counts. For 𝑁 = 4109 tokens, ignoring incomplete chunks and sequence-start masking, token-level targets require 𝑁 queries and chunk-level targets require 𝑁/32. Retrieving 1,024 versus 16 neighbors yields 1024𝑁 versus 16𝑁/32 returned slots. Their ratios are 32 for queries and 2048 for returned slots. The latter counts search outputs before MLP Memory removes the self neighbor and aggregates token probabilities. It does not count distinct tokens, search candidates examined, stored bytes, or FLOPs: DFMs continuous vector targets differ from token-level distribution targets.

sections.title: Deep Fusion Memory
sections.content: E. Case Studies E.1. Question Answering Figure 5 compares answers from Base, MLP Memory, and DFM on six selected HotpotQA examples using Mistral-7B-v0.3. DFM answers all six correctly, while Base and MLP Memory give the same incorrect answer in each case. DFM identifies Manglietia from the stated species count and geographic origin, whereas both baselines choose Abronia. For the film comparison, DFM correctly selects What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?, while both baselines select All the Marbles. The other four cases cover shared property of two bands, composers nationality, universitys association with cartoon character, and the film underlying Pixar short. Cases were selected for correct normalized exact match from DFM and zero exact match, substring match, and F1 from both baselines. MLP Memory uses 𝜆 = 0.55. These selected successes illustrate differences in final answers, without establishing their frequency or revealing the models intermediate reasoning. Figure 5 Six selected HotpotQA answer comparisons using Mistral-7B-v0.3. Columns show Base (left), MLP Memory (middle), and DFM (right). Check and cross symbols indicate correct and incorrect normalized exact-match answers.

sections.title: Deep Fusion Memory
sections.content: E.2. Offline Retrieval Supervision Figure 6 presents seven examples of the offline retrieval used to construct training targets. Each row pairs preceding 32-token query chunk with retrieved chunk text and the ground-truth next chunk. For Pakenham, the retrieved text supplies the network operator, Metro Trains Melbourne. For Bhutan cricket, it supplies the 2001 ICC membership and international debut. The other cases cover chart position, railway privatization, Welsh place names, mountain range, and legal proceeding. Highlighted spans identify continuation-relevant information that is missing or incomplete in the query chunk. The selected records exclude the query chunk itself, exact query-text matches, and chunks from the same source block. Cross-block near duplicates may remain. These examples illustrate the relevance of retrieved supervision targets. They do not directly measure the fidelity of predicted memory or attribute the answer differences above to particular retrieved chunks. Figure 6 Seven selected offline retrieval examples. Each row shows the preceding query chunk, retrieved chunk text, and ground-truth continuation. Brown spans mark continuation-relevant information in the retrieved text. Text is shortened for display, and split words preserve chunk boundaries.
